records.name: South Gyeongsang
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): conservative south-east. Scored relative to the national score (0.71) for South Korea. The country dossier located no province-specific trans ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for this division; all three sources below are national-context legal and survey material that applies province-wide.

sources.claim: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award (against a 3 million won claim), ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female - who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 - to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The article also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents (41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink, 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. This is the national framework this province is scored against; no KOR/South Gyeongsang-specific incident appears.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria; the court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the framework this province is scored against; the wire contains no KOR/South Gyeongsang-specific content.

records.name: Busan
records.current_summary:
Nothing in the audited sources documents a region-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern concerning trans people in this metropolitan area. The framework a visitor stands under is the national one: trans status is not criminalised; legal gender recognition exists but its medical prerequisites were struck down by a May 2024 court ruling; and in July 2024 a court held that police who advised a trans person to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, awarding damages after two instances ruled for the claimant, with the appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

The same ruling's report adds the practical picture from national data: a 2021 human-rights commission survey of 591 trans respondents found fear-driven restroom avoidance routine (41% using mismatched facilities, 36% foregoing them), and a 2021 damages award went against an academy that barred a trans student from its restrooms. Audited evidence therefore supports legality, functioning judicial recourse and social ambivalence over facilities here; the audited record documents nothing about this city, favourable or unfavourable, that distinguishes it from that nationwide picture.
records.current_localsOnly: A January 2024 study of 208 LGBTQ students in schools here found 39% reported mistreatment (outing, teasing, insults, condemnation, violence) because of gender identity or sexual orientation — school environments bear on residents and enrolled students, not foreign visitors.

records.name: Jeju
records.current_summary:
No region-specific law, incident or enforcement finding about trans people exists in the audited record for this island, and the national framework applies: trans status is not criminalised; a May 2024 ruling removed surgical requirements for changing registered sex; and the July 2024 damages judgment against police advice that a transitioning person avoid public restrooms — with its appellate language on restroom use as a fundamental and universal human right — governs here as in the rest of the country. The same sources' national survey data (2021: large majorities of trans respondents reporting fear-driven facility avoidance) and a 2021 damages award for a student barred from academy restrooms describe the practical baseline.

An earlier characterisation of this island as the country's most permissive region was a model prior, not a finding; it is not supported by any surviving audited source and has been removed. What the record can support for a visitor is the national position on this island — lawful status, available courts, social ambivalence about facilities — and no locally documented fact making this island safer or harsher than that picture.

records.name: Sejong
records.current_summary:
The audited sources document no region-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding touching trans people in this administratively special city; what governs a visitor is the national framework: trans status is lawful; surgery cannot be required to amend registered sex after a May 2024 ruling; and in July 2024 a court awarded damages holding that police advice to a transitioning person to avoid public restrooms infringed personal rights, the appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right. The same record carries national survey data (2021) showing fear-driven restroom avoidance among trans respondents and a 2021 damages award for a student excluded from a private academy's facilities.

Whether the concentration of government agencies here changes official climate for trans residents or visitors is not documented in the audited record — neither protective nor hostile initiatives are recorded — so the city's visitor-facing facts reduce to the national framework and its documented social friction over public facilities.

records.name: Atlántico
records.current_summary:
Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 annual report issues a specific, named warning of "increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the Atlántico department," and quantifies it: 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats and 8 lethal-violence cases in the department, with 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders; the report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories at "high" threat level. Barranquilla is the Caribbean-coast hub for trans sex work and the city where the NGO's documentation base operates, giving it both elevated exposure and visibility in monitoring data; the department appears explicitly in the 270-victim national total (+63% on 2024; one killing every 32 hours). Impunity is near-total nationally: 99.8% of threat cases never advanced past the investigation stage. A positive institutional signal is recorded: the department's development plan (and Barranquilla's) commits coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violent acts against LGBTIQ+ people.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Atlántico falls approximately 0.09 lower, justified by the NGO's named escalation warning (not merely inclusion in aggregate counts, but a specific "increase" call-out) and the structural role of Barranquilla's trans sex-work corridor. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Atlántico is higher: its violence is a rising trend flagged by Caribe Afirmativo rather than the decade-deep, impunity-saturated lethality concentration that makes Antioquia "one of the most dangerous" in Colombia. Versus Bolívar (0.44), Atlántico sits marginally lower because its finding is a forward-looking escalation warning tied to a specific urban hub, whereas Bolívar's deviation rests on one targeted killing of a named community leader.
records.current_localsOnly: The 54 intrafamily-violence cases, the two killings of community defenders and the digital-violence/doxxing displacement documented for 2025 are resident- and activist-facing rather than visitor-directed; the visitor-facing risk signal is the public-space lethality, impunity and named high-threat designation for the department's main hub.

sources.claim: Publimetro Colombia (27 September 2026) on Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia': nationally 270 victims in 2025, a 63% increase over 2024 (165 homicides), one killing every 32 hours. For the Atlántico department it documents 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases, and designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories with 'high' threat levels for this population; it recalls the department's and Barranquilla's development plans commit coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people. It also reports threats show near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage.

Caribe Afirmativo's own 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia': in 2025 one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours, and violence runs a continuum from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity; the report documents territorial expansion of the violence, including towards territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and criticises the insufficient state response. The cached text does not break out Atlántico-specific counts (those are carried by the companion Publimetro piece); it underpins the national crisis-scale and territorial-expansion claims this record is scored against.
